section.title: Mozilla Firefox CTO: Chrome vs Firefox, Distinguished Engineers, and the AI Browser Wars
section.deck: Bobby Holly traces Firefox's fight with Chrome and Google, explains how Mozilla defines distinguished-engineer impact, and argues for impact over titles and for keeping the web open as AI arrives.

blocks.text: Bobby Holly, who grew from a Mozilla intern into the CTO of Firefox, argues that engineers should chase the biggest problems and real impact rather than titles, and that the web's open, multi-vendor character is worth defending against Chrome's dominance and the rush to put AI into browsers. The conversation runs from Holly's start in Mozilla's volunteer-heavy open-source culture, through the browser wars with Google, security crises, the Rust and Servo bet and the Quantum CSS launch, to Holly's views on promotions, distinguished engineers, writing, and the future of the browser. Every claim, estimate and recollection below is Holly's own. The host is not named in the transcript.
blocks.heading: Holly's view: pursue impact, not titles, and keep the web open and independent

blocks.question: Before joining Firefox you interned at Nvidia. Why did you pick Mozilla over Nvidia?
answer: Holly describes the Nvidia internship as a good, standard one: orientation, a desk, a basic starter project and check-ins every few hours. Mozilla was quite different. On the first day Holly's manager, the director of platform who ran Gecko, was extremely laid-back and, asked what to work on, said to get on IRC and Bugzilla and start figuring something out.

Holly says that reflected how Mozilla worked. It had grown as an open-source project partly by accident, with almost no support, so newcomers had to work out for themselves how to download the code, build it and file bugs. That selected for highly motivated people, and management's job was to nurture the culture, get the right people together and get out of the way. Holly found it disorienting at first and then inspired by the people, some paid and some not, who had started out in college dorm rooms trying to make their browser crash less.

A long-time hero was Boris Sabarski, whom Holly says became one of Mozilla's first distinguished engineers. Holly describes a codebase of probably about 10 million lines inherited from Netscape and largely unowned, of which Boris owned perhaps half and was the person of last resort. For years Holly met him only on IRC, where he was in about five other channels at once.

followups.question: How does this fit the timeline of Chrome and the browser wars? Was this before Chrome?
answer: Holly says it was before Chrome and gives a short history. In the 1990s Internet Explorer beat Netscape, largely because Microsoft bundled it free with Windows and pushed hard on distribution. Netscape open-sourced its code and created the Mozilla Foundation, while Microsoft put the browser in maintenance mode because a cross-platform web did not fit its strategy. Contributors such as Boris kept improving the Netscape code, adding pop-up blocking and tabs, until a few relatively junior people built a stripped-down browser that became Firefox and, Holly says, took off like wildfire.

Google was closely aligned, Holly says, because a search company benefits when the web is useful. When Holly started in June 2008, interns had badges to eat at Google, Google's default-search deal made Mozilla financially sustainable, and Google engineers worked on Firefox. Soon after, Google announced Chrome, and Mozilla staff were told it was still friendly and aimed at Internet Explorer. By 2009, Holly recalls, a New York Times article described group hugs between Mozilla and Google as getting tricky, as Google's business interest in controlling the user's journey created tension.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: How did things move from Google badges and free food to full competition, in your own experience?
answer: Holly does not think any individual at Google decided to go after Mozilla. It was the way organizations work, and collaboration with many Google engineers continued. Two things happened at once. First, Google ramped up its push for Chrome share. Holly says this was probably aimed at Internet Explorer, with Mozilla as collateral damage, and estimates Google spent hundreds of millions of dollars a year on advertising and distribution, reaching into the billions if promotion on google.com is counted.

Holly cites Jonathan Nightingale, then a Firefox vice president, who later described a 'year of 100 oopses': each time Google did something that hurt Firefox, such as putting a banner on google.com telling Firefox users to download Chrome, it was framed as unintentional. Holly believes that was true at the organizational level, but that individual incentives rewarded it, since a fix weeks later still left the metrics won.

Second, Holly says Firefox had legitimately fallen behind. Chrome arrived with a multiprocess architecture, a more robust plug-in architecture for Adobe Flash, and a very fast JavaScript engine. Mozilla also made an ambitious early-2010s bet on a web-based mobile operating system, Firefox OS, because Android and iOS looked potentially hostile. It drew surprising industry interest but did not work, and it competed for resources with keeping Firefox competitive. Firefox's extension model was a further drag: extensions could modify almost anything and depended on undocumented internals, so nearly any change risked breaking one.

followups.question: Why did people spend so much time working for free on a project like this?
answer: Holly says there were few major open-source projects then, so Mozilla offered a chance to have meaningful impact. Boris got involved because, as Holly tells it, his options for browsing from an MIT dorm were a remote Internet Explorer 5 session or a Netscape build that kept crashing, so he set out to fix it for himself and found the codebase a vast intellectual challenge.

The biggest factor, in Holly's view, was the mission: the web should be open, interoperable and controlled by no single company, and the internet should be a global public resource. Holly argues that was not a given for anyone who grew up in the 1990s with Microsoft dominant. Mozilla was not only advocating but building a browser that gave users pop-up blocking, ad blocking and tabs, and Holly says that inspired many people.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: Once you got there, which projects were most interesting or shaped your career, and what stories come from the early days?
answer: Holly started as an intern on the front end of a new mobile browser for Nokia devices, then worked on the graphics engine and image rendering library. Because so much code was unowned, fixing one thing quickly led to hearing that Holly now owned it. Holly gravitated to the hardest and gnarliest parts, especially after Chrome launched with the V8 JIT-compiled JavaScript engine. Shipping Firefox's own JIT was delayed by months for Firefox 4 because of the tangled bindings between the JavaScript engine and the DOM, and Holly dived into that code at the manager's advice.

That code carried much of the browser's security enforcement, isolating websites from each other and from the browser's own JavaScript front end. Holly says it was imperfect and became a cat-and-mouse game with outside security researchers, in which a clever trick could climb the prototype chain into the address bar and tab code. After Firefox 4 improved the architecture, Holly worried that some categories of attack had no robust fix, only band-aids, and launched a cross-functional effort of at least a year, jokingly called Slaughterhouse, to remove the Chrome object wrappers. Mozilla paid small bounties for confidential Bugzilla reports, though the black market paid more.

Holly's main story involves a zero-day exploit in the wild. While disassembling it, Holly realized it was written by a researcher Mozilla worked with and, without thinking hard, emailed an accusation of double-crossing. The researcher concluded his own devices were deeply compromised and went off the grid. About an hour later Mozilla learned the real cause: a threat actor had compromised Bugzilla. Weeks later the researcher phoned from a bowling alley in upstate New York where he was hiding, and Mozilla explained and helped him recover. Slaughterhouse had just wrapped, and of roughly 45 exfiltrated bugs by Holly's recollection, all but two were already fixed. Holly's lesson is to get ahead of security and architecture, because sometimes you do not have time to fix things when you need to.

followups.question: How did you know that researcher wrote that exploit?
answer: Holly says people have particular styles, and these were handwritten logic attacks, for example binding a function to an API and sending a call around the event loop twice, so the fingerprints were visible. Holly separates these from memory-safety vulnerabilities, which were less artisanal and more often produced by fuzzing tools. Because the codebase was C++, a memory hazard could mean a web page takes over the computer, and Holly says this motivated Mozilla's investment in Rust.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

followups.question: How does a Firefox compromise take over the computer? Wouldn't the operating system shield it?
answer: Not at the time, Holly says. Windows applications largely ran with system privileges, and researchers proved a compromise by launching the Windows calculator. Chrome helped raise the baseline, and today's browsers use defense in depth, including in-process and operating-system sandboxing. But Holly says this was bolted on over time on Windows, unlike iOS, which was designed around application sandboxing, so securing browsers there remains an ongoing challenge.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

followups.question: Did you ever work out how Bugzilla was compromised?
answer: Holly is about 85 percent sure it was a leaked employee credential, before Bugzilla, a tool dating to the 1990s, had two-factor authentication.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: How does the organization prioritize security when there were also big investments in performance?
answer: Holly says security is easy to neglect for short-term reasons, and some products may reasonably do so, but a long-lived browser cannot. At Mozilla it is a cultural obligation to protect users that predates management structure or company objectives, and it produces bottom-up energy and pride. Holly puts Chrome's security organization at 70 or more people; Mozilla has nothing close, so security is a shared responsibility. Slaughterhouse was not a top-down edict, Holly says. Holly owned the code and felt it had to be right.

Holly is proud that Firefox has won the Pwn2Own award for fastest to patch, on the order of 24 hours, for the last two years. That relies on people in time zones around the world working without any management instruction to stay up late, simply because they care. Holly notes that every browser gets compromised in that competition.

followups.question: You mentioned no performance reviews and a scrappy bottom-up culture. How does that kind of culture work?
answer: Before there was much management, Holly says, it was uneven. It generally worked because the caliber of people was high, but if the owner of some code did a poor job, everyone lived with it. Ownership was treated as close to final, and Mozilla's module system and governance were insulated against executive power. Holly thinks parts of that culture are worth preserving and describes the leadership question as how to keep what makes the technical culture great while addressing its shortcomings.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: How did Mozilla adopt Rust, and how does it solve the memory-safety problem?
answer: Holly says that in the early 2010s Firefox had real structural issues. Many could be solved by hard but incremental work: a multiprocess architecture, an extension architecture without tendrils into undocumented interfaces, and native video playback to escape Flash. Two issues were different. One was memory safety, because in a C++ codebase a large share of mistakes compromise the browser and, without sandboxing, the computer.

The other was parallelism. Core counts were rising while browsers stayed largely single-threaded, but multithreaded C++ produced hard nondeterministic bugs that could also become exploitable. Holly says both problems were rooted in deficiencies of C++, which every browser used. Firefox had just taken on the world in 2010, so Mozilla began sponsoring internal research into a new language with compile-time guarantees of no memory-safety issues and no race conditions, to be followed by a new browser engine. Rust co-evolved with Servo, a test bed meant to be memory safe and, more importantly, parallel, so that Mozilla could close the gap with Chrome and leapfrog it through safe concurrency.
blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: What was Mozilla's strategy to compete with Chrome, given its performance and distribution advantages?
answer: Holly calls it multifaceted. The first part was recognition. Holly says there was early denial about the value of Chrome's architectural advantages. Chrome had a method JIT while Firefox had a tracing JIT that Mozilla expected to be better and was not. When Chrome shipped a multiprocess architecture, the first reaction Holly heard was good luck doing that on Mac, and then Chrome did it. On video, Chrome had a better Flash plug-in architecture and was early with native playback, so YouTube was stable there while Firefox crashed constantly, which Holly says was Adobe's fault and not fixable by Mozilla. So Mozilla had to close many hard, discrete gaps, but closing the gap was not enough. It had to do something better, and Rust and Servo were the strategy for that.

followups.question: How did the Servo effort go? Was it successful, given that Google's distribution eventually dominated?
answer: Holly says Servo and Rust had captured something real. Servo was an incomplete prototype but had features never done before, including a multithreaded CSS engine. The problem was scale: about a dozen people on Rust and Servo against hundreds of Chromium engineers, with most of Mozilla's effort still on Gecko. A competitive engine is years of accumulated work, so Servo had more to catch up on every year, and Holly found it hard to believe it would ever match a production engine.

Around 2014 to 2015 Mozilla concluded it needed a fully refreshed Firefox, including the parallel CSS engine uplifted from Servo, a project Holly personally led and calls the highlight of the career. Hooking a Rust CSS engine to the C++ DOM had no tooling, so the team built it. Holly recalls rendering time on Amazon.com improving by on the order of 25 percent, and says the engine, being parallel, is still the fastest on the market. Firefox was performance-competitive again, and Holly's lesson is that coordinated technical effort and the right bets can win.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: Where were you in your career at that point, and how did it grow as you worked on these projects?
answer: Holly says early Mozilla had a choose-your-own-title culture, and Holly chose 'negative entropy' for the complex codebase. By Firefox Quantum, Mozilla had a more standard ladder. Holly had reached senior staff during Quantum CSS, and after launch Holly and the engineer who led the other half of Quantum were promoted to principal engineer, a level held by probably fewer than five people at the time by Holly's estimate.

Holly's long-term dream was to be like Boris Sabarski, one of Mozilla's three distinguished engineers, and the route was to be prolific across as many parts of the code as possible: WebRender, mobile, multiprocess, layout. Holly's manager, who ran engineering, asked Holly to spend one day a week not opening a terminal and to think about impact more broadly than direct code. Holly was shocked and says it was not a natural way to work.

followups.question: Do you have a way of thinking about which contributions are more impactful than others?
answer: Holly says it was a guided search for the biggest problem on offer, which changed over time: DOM bindings and security, then media playback to solve the YouTube problem, multiprocess, the Rust-based CSS engine, WebRender, and then mobile. Holly's model was to jump into the most pressing area, learn its code and work with its leaders, not always typing the code but reviewing, setting direction and setting priorities. The host summarizes this as prolific but aimed at the organization's biggest problems, and Holly agrees.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: In the industry I hear two approaches to growth: focus on the promotion first, or build skills and behaviors and let the promotion follow. Which is better?
answer: Holly has strong opinions and says to focus on impact, not title. That is what Holly looks for when deciding whom to advance. Someone having that level of impact does not need to sell themselves the way promo hacking implies, which means pinning down a management chain on exactly what must be done to earn a promotion.

Speaking frankly, Holly finds that annoying, comparing it to a child asking for a reward in exchange for doing what was asked. Holly also sees a substantive problem. A person focused on impact will achieve things, whereas a person focused on boxes someone else presented may technically satisfy a stated condition in a box-checking way that misses the point. Impact is what should be recognized and rewarded.

followups.question: Softer-spoken engineers often do great work but market it poorly. Brag documents and sharing wins seem a reasonable balance. How do you weigh the two framings?
answer: Holly says similar activities can be framed several ways, and the framing shapes how they are carried out and what they achieve. Visibility is a basic fact of impact: you need to be connected to people who understand the biggest challenges, coordinate with them, and make sure they know what you can do so they can put you in a position to do more. But Holly says trying to brag and trying to communicate, coordinate and create visibility for important work lead to very different outcomes.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

followups.question: The wording of an update can be subtle, and the same post can come from different incentives. Can people tell?
answer: Holly says much depends on how much the update is about you versus the work, the team and other people. Everyone knows the sender likely had a significant hand in the work, so an important part of any update is giving visibility to others and thanking the team. Holly sees that as part of leadership: being a humble leader who creates recognition for other people's contributions.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

followups.question: Doesn't the squeaky wheel get the grease? A loud high performer who lobbies for promotion is often rewarded before a quiet, solid one.
answer: Holly says it depends on the organization and its technical culture, and Mozilla tries hard not to reward that. The message is not to avoid ambition but to frame it as the impact you want, not the status you want. Holly allows that in edge cases people lobbying for themselves get a little more consideration because they are top of mind.

The conversations Holly likes best are about how to grow and have more impact, such as whether you are working on the most important thing. Holly calls it the saddest outcome when someone works very hard on something not important enough to give the impact they want. Pinning leaders down on which boxes to check is, Holly says, extremely annoying, and you do not want leadership to find you annoying.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: You were focused on impact and had distinguished engineers as role models. What did the growth look like next?
answer: Holly kept working on the hardest challenge in the browser and moving from team to team, assuming that Boris Sabarski's level of impact would eventually mean becoming a distinguished engineer. Then the CTO at the time sat Holly down. The existing distinguished engineers had held the title since about 2010 and no new ones had been made since. The CTO said Mozilla would make new ones for the first time in almost a decade and that Holly would not be among them.

Holly was a little surprised, since Holly thought anyone would say that, though perhaps not at Boris's level, Holly knew the Firefox code better than almost anyone. The CTO explained that this was the traditional Mozilla model and that he now wanted something oriented around industry impact.

followups.question: The definition of impact shifted while you were working toward distinguished engineer. What was your thinking about the new criteria?
answer: Holly found it inspiring, though some people worried Holly would be upset. Holly compares it to doing a new Pilates move and discovering a muscle you did not know you had and that is extremely weak. What defines a distinguished engineer, Holly says, depends on what matters to the organization. Early on, Mozilla's make-or-break problem was managing a sprawling codebase with few people, which called for a prolific contributor and enabler. At some companies the title means building a billion-dollar business, but Mozilla is about changing the world, so its criteria focus there.

Holly says Holly probably still has not reached the industry impact of some of Mozilla's other distinguished engineers, and that the eventual promotion was a hybrid of the old and new definitions. But understanding that model of impact was profound and shaped where Holly directed effort.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: What does distinguished-engineer-level impact look like? Can you describe some people who have done impressive work?
answer: Holly describes three engineers promoted at the time as archetypes of world-changing impact for an individual contributor at Mozilla.

The first is Martin Thompson, still at Mozilla, whom Holly calls an international standards extraordinaire. His name is in the author line of protocols such as HTTP/2, QUIC and web push, and Holly says he was heavily involved in WebRTC and geolocation, adding that Holly is not familiar with every credit. This was core design work, not editorial formatting. By designing new protocols that were faster, giving the industry a business reason to adopt them, while leaking less metadata and having fewer security issues, he increased the privacy and security of the internet.

The second is Luke Wagner, whom Holly considers the person most single-handedly responsible for WebAssembly. Running non-JavaScript code such as AutoCAD in browsers had relied on plugins, which Holly calls awful for security and user experience. A side project from another engineer compiled C++ to naive JavaScript, which worked but was very slow. Wagner, then a lead engineer on the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine, wanted it viable, and the idea became having the tool emit a restricted subset of JavaScript the engine could detect, verify and run more natively. That started a flywheel of compiled native experiences in browsers and then momentum for a real bytecode format, WebAssembly, which is native-speed, sandboxed and portable. Google was pushing a plugin-like alternative, Native Client, so Wagner handled the technical and political pieces to forge a browser consensus.

The third is Tim Terbury, the codec lead. Native video playback was blocked because the dominant format, H.264, was heavily patent-encumbered, which an open-source browser could not ship. Mozilla spent years developing royalty-free codecs. Terbury's team built the Opus audio codec and then a video codec called Daala, which was incorporated into AV1, now an industry standard from the Alliance for Open Media. Holly says that powers video today and that the vision for truly unencumbered codecs came from Terbury.

followups.question: The value these engineers created is huge, with WebAssembly making a company like Figma possible, but the value is captured elsewhere. Does that bother people at Mozilla?
answer: Holly says Mozilla has no shareholders and is not trying to make gobs of money. Its mission is an internet that is open and accessible to all. Holly grants it is convenient for big tech companies to have a royalty-free codec, but notes they could pay. Mozilla's angle is to build formats that empower everybody and create economic value, even though some capture more than others.

Holly adds that Mozilla wants to keep existing, which means thinking about revenue, and a lot of its revenue comes from Google, one of the dominant advertising players. Mozilla would like to change that, but it is hard and not where its heart is, so Holly describes a real tension about how much to focus on business versus impact.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: What advice would you give someone who wants to become a distinguished engineer?
answer: Holly's answer is writing, which anyone can work on at any level. Holly says Mozilla, including Holly personally, did not have much developed capability here, and that writing is one of the most powerful skills. Holly points to an internal memo, now public, called 'writing things down', which argues that writing matters both for the artifact, which helps coordination, wide review and feedback, and for the process, since writing is thinking, refining and articulating ideas. Holly calls clarity of thinking one of the most important things and says you only get it by forcing yourself to write your ideas down.
As timely advice, Holly says not to use an LLM to produce text you put your name on. It is fairly easy to tell, and more importantly you lose the thinking that writing forces.

followups.question: Do you have tips on how to write well?
answer: Holly says a document should be no longer than what you have to say. When you run out of things to say, you either refine your ideas or you are done, because fluff is never useful and padded documents are among Holly's least favorite things. Focus on substance over rhetoric. Holly rejects the idea that non-native English speakers cannot write as well as others: there is a baseline of articulation to work on, but good writing is not flowery words. It is clarity of thought, which is relatively easy to express once you have it, if you practice.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: As CTO of Firefox, what do you expect from the new browser wars, with AI browsers and AI being added to existing browsers?
answer: Holly says the new AI browsers announced each month are not browsers as Holly thinks of them. They are different front ends, window dressing and monetization keys on top of Chrome, because much of what powers a browser is the engine, and engines are extremely hard to build and have been disappearing. Holly says Firefox, built on Gecko, is the only independent browser with no dependency on someone else's engine. Safari is vertically integrated with WebKit, and Chrome, Opera, Perplexity and Edge all use Chromium. Holly argues these companies are not trying to evolve the web platform but to control the consumer touchpoint in the coming AI world.

Holly's view is that AI is coming to consumer technology 'like water running downhill' and will not be stopped, but where it ends up can still be steered, and many parties want to capture it. Holly says Chrome is making an aggressive play to control the AI stack, both in the browser, with what Holly describes as thousands of Gemini integrations, and in the web platform, through proprietary APIs Mozilla does not support that let websites use an LLM inside the browser. Site authors like this because they can offload inference costs. But there is no way to specify an LLM or give it deterministic, interoperable behavior, so these calls are fundamentally unspecified, and as owner of the dominant browser Google has the market power to get websites to tune their usage to what Gemini expects.

Holly says Mozilla is not building a foundation model and has no horse in the race. It wants the space to stay open, users to choose which AI systems they use, and the web to remain relevant. Holly sees a real risk that the web becomes a backend detail used by retrieval behind a ChatGPT query or by an agent. Much would be lost, Holly argues, because the web gives users agency: it is reinterpretable content the browser can modify as the user chooses, as ad blockers show, it is safe to open a link from an untrusted source, and no one company controls it. Holly calls this multistakeholder structure a historical accident that matches Mozilla's vision, and wants AI's changes not to sacrifice it.

followups.question: Many AI browsers and Opera are built on Chromium. What would happen if Firefox were built on Chromium, and what is the advantage of its own engine?
answer: Holly says it is a lot of work and Mozilla likes hard things, but the advantage is a seat at the table when web standards are decided. Engines have dropped off because from a bottom-line view an engine is a giant cost center. Mozilla keeps going because it is driven by impact. Holly pictures a world with Apple running WebKit and Google in charge of everything else: both capable, but entrenched in their own interests and not getting along, and bilateral entrenchment can prevent progress, as in mobile. Despite a smaller share, Mozilla brings a fresh perspective and can tilt the conversation back toward the user and the web.

Holly's example is performance. Historically each vendor designed a benchmark suited to its own engine and the others dismissed it as cooked. A couple of years ago an initiative called Speedometer 3 aimed to produce a shared benchmark representative of the web. Holly says a bilateral Google and Apple effort would predictably go nowhere, and that Mozilla's involvement kept everyone focused on making engines faster together. By Holly's account Firefox and Chrome have each doubled their score, and in Firefox the measured effect on real-world page load and time to first paint was about 30 percent, so Holly judges it reasonable to say the benchmark made the web 30 percent faster, which would not have happened without Mozilla in the room.
followups.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: You were an IC through and through for most of your time at Mozilla. Is there a technical decision you wish you had changed in hindsight?
answer: Holly points to a case where the technical outcome was good but the process was not worth it: WebRender, the graphics backend in Servo. While working on Quantum CSS, Holly was excited about uplifting more of Servo's rendering pipeline and advocated heavily that the graphics team replace its rendering and rasterization pipeline with Servo's. Holly says this was not based on technical expertise in that area but on a vibes judgment about where things were going, and the vibes were infectious. Holly was not strictly a decision-maker, but the view caught on with management.

Many engineers on the graphics team had strong doubts that it was ready or that it was too risky. When they raised concerns, Holly recalls, an engineering leader replied that C++ is not the future. Holly says enthusiasm for a risky direction over the concerns of the people who knew the area best was toxic, and several of the most senior and impactful graphics engineers left. The rest rallied, and WebRender became a major, expensive, many-year project. Holly stresses that the result is a fantastic, performant and safe engine and that Holly is proud of the team. But pushing it on a team that was not ready or aligned had collateral damage that Holly regrets.
blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: Is there a top book that made an impact on your career?
answer: Holly says Holly is an avid reader who does not read many books, and that the ideas that most shaped Holly's thinking come from books Holly has not actually read. Holly consumes content widely and sees reading a whole book as a depth-first approach. That works for many people, but it is not the only way.

As examples, Holly read only a three-page review of Good Strategy, Bad Strategy, and says it stuck as a crisp account of what is wrong with many strategy documents. Holly also cites Turn the Ship Around, unread, on empowering teams, and Clayton Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma as a powerful analysis of how the industry works. Holly values Ben Thompson's writing on tech but urges people to look beyond tech, for example to geopolitics and national security writing by people who think about what goes well and badly on a battlefield. Holly says those ideas rhyme with big-tech competition and with how to manage and motivate teams.
blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: If you could give yourself advice when you had just entered the industry, what would it be?
answer: Holly's answer is to be humble. Holly says the younger attitude was not strictly about self but about engineering, that engineers were the center of the universe. Over time Holly realized that many other things matter, and that when you start at an organization you do not understand why certain processes and functions exist, such as a legal team. Moving into leadership, Holly developed appreciation and empathy for the different players in the organization and industry, recognizing that everyone has a point of view and a place they are coming from, and that working to understand where people are coming from is how to make progress.
blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

blocks.question: Do you have any last words for the audience?
answer: Holly's main message is that the web matters and underpins much of what we do, even though for many it is invisible and taken for granted, like water from the tap or the semiconductor supply chain. Holly warns it could easily backslide into unilateral big-tech control over people's experiences, and that losing focus because it has been good for so long would be a tragedy. Holly encourages people to think about what they gain from an open and free web and to do their best to keep it open.

Holly's practical request is that people building websites make sure they work in all browsers and avoid the lazy path of building something that works only in Google Chrome, which Holly calls the first step back to where things stood 25 years ago.
blocks.speaker: Bobby Holly

coverage.reason: Read all 8 compact chunks in full (about 95 minutes, 2,424 caption snippets). Kept 16 initiating rounds and 15 follow-ups in source order, with follow-ups nested under the question they answer. Several host questions are lightly condensed from captions that merge host and guest turns; speaker turns were separated by reading, so some boundaries are approximate. Holly's figures are recollections or estimates and are unverified: about 10 million lines inherited from Netscape, ad spend of hundreds of millions to billions of dollars, about 45 exfiltrated Bugzilla bugs, 85 percent confidence on the credential-leak cause, about 25 percent Amazon.com rendering gain from Quantum CSS, fewer than five principal engineers, a Chrome security organization of 70 plus, a roughly 30 percent real-world gain tied to Speedometer 3, and the claim that Firefox won Pwn2Own fastest-to-patch for two years. The spoken claim of 5,000 Gemini integrations in Chrome is rendered loosely as thousands. Names follow the auto-generated captions and may be misspelled, including Bobby Holly, Boris Sabarski, Tim Terbury, Jonathan Nightingale and the Daala codec; the tools behind WebAssembly, the Mozilla CTO and the managers were garbled in captions and are described without names.
